Dermatology · published research

Lichen planopilaris

Small uncontrolled reports describe reduced inflammation or symptoms and some hair-thickness gains, but they do not establish that PBM prevents permanent follicle loss. An ex-vivo study found no significant gene-expression change in the LLLT arm.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small uncontrolled reports describe reduced inflammation or symptoms and some hair-thickness gains, but they do not establish that PBM prevents permanent follicle loss. An ex-vivo study found no significant gene-expression change in the LLLT arm.

Summary of the Evidence

Four publications are relevant when three exact lichen planopilaris records are combined with one mixed scarring-alopecia pilot that directly included eight people with lichen planopilaris. The exact-category reports comprise small case series and case-level evidence; the mapped pilot enrolled 16 people, including eight with lichen planopilaris and eight with frontal fibrosing alopecia. A separate 2025 study analyzed scalp biopsies before and after treatment. The publications do not establish whether all patient samples were independent, and there is no randomized controlled trial directly testing PBM for this condition.

Human and clinical evidence

An early case series described less scalp redness, perifollicular scale, itching, and disease activity during treatment. The mean Lichen Planopilaris Activity Index decreased at six months, although the improvement was not maintained at the later follow-up; measurements also showed increased terminal-hair thickness at months three and six (Fonda-Pascual et al. 2017).

A mixed-cohort pilot reported a decrease in disease activity among its eight lichen planopilaris participants and an increase in thick hairs. Participants also received ongoing care, and there was no untreated comparison group, so the change cannot be assigned to PBM alone (Gerkowicz et al. 2019). A later four-patient case series described reduced symptoms and inflammation during red-light treatment; patients remained on treatment during the observation period, so sustained control after stopping is not known (Randolph et al. 2020).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly relevant to lichen planopilaris was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

A 2025 study compared scalp-biopsy gene expression before and after six months of hydroxychloroquine, narrowband UVB, or low-level laser light therapy. It did not identify significant differentially expressed genes in the laser arm. This laboratory measurement does not rule out a clinical effect, but it does not provide a molecular change supporting one either (Yıldız-Altay et al. 2025).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Reports used red visible light around 630–660 nm. Protocols ranged from daily use over several months to weekly sessions over ten weeks; one mixed pilot reported approximately 44.45 J/cm² per session. Differences in device, dose, treatment schedule, ongoing medication, and outcome measurement make direct comparisons difficult. The studies do not establish an optimal dose or show that short-term symptom change prevents permanent scarring.

Interpretation

The clinical reports describe improvements in symptoms, visible inflammation, activity scores, or hair thickness in some patients. These are useful early observations, but the uncontrolled designs cannot show that PBM caused the changes or prevented lasting follicle loss. Evidence for symptom or activity improvement is stronger than evidence for regrowth or long-term disease modification.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term reduction in disease activity and symptoms Very low for hair regrowth or prevention of permanent scarring
Publications and records4 articles (one mixed-diagnosis pilot mapped)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Small reports describe lower activity scores, fewer symptoms, and some increases in thicker hairs, so these observations are worth reporting. They are mostly uncontrolled, and the mixed-diagnosis pilot included another scarring alopecia. The biopsy study found no significant gene-expression change in its laser arm. A controlled trial with standardized activity scores, hair counts, and longer follow-up would be needed for stronger conclusions.
